subject: lavaGolem
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: lava golem of basalt plates and molten seams.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm planning a lava golem design—a hulking basalt humanoid with glowing molten seams, a crystalline chest core, spiked pauldrons, and a horned crest, aiming for a Genshin-style aesthetic.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy (hips, spine, chest, neck, head, with jointed arms and legs) and setting proportions for a roughly 3-meter-tall figure, then defining a basalt and lava color palette and building procedural paint functions using noise and cell patterns to create glowing cracked-rock surfaces.

Writing paint logic...

For the body, I'm thinking blocky torso built along a spine chain with rounded box or sweep cross-sections, going with a sweep approach using box-like sections and a radius function for that chunky golem shape.

I'm sketching the spine chain's path through four knots from hips up to chest, naming the joints spine1, spine2, and chest, and double-checking the point count lines up with the number of bone spans so the rig deforms cleanly.

For the neck and head, I'm deciding whether to use a two-point chain producing a tip joint for the head, versus just defining a standalone head joint explicitly with its own orientation so it faces forward properly for attaching the jaw as a child.

Setting up head's local axes...

Still placing jaw geometry... I'm sizing the lower jaw box and adding a thin glowing lava slab between the jaws, plus small cones for teeth along the jaw line.

Now I'm figuring out eye placement, defining the skull as a box with specific width, height, and depth centered on the head joint, then positioning angled glowing eye slits on its front face using local coordinates.

Adding a tilted brow ridge and angled brow boxes above the eyes for an angry expression, then working out how to attach backward-swept basalt horn spikes to the skull using directional vectors and radius parameters.

Still writing horn geometry... I'm swapping to curved bezier sweeps for the horns with molten lava-tipped bands near the points, then starting on a glowing flame-shaped crest extruded along the top of the head.

Now I'm sketching out the torso: sweeping a box cross-section along the spine chain, with radii tapering from wide hips down through a narrower belly to a broader chest near the top.

I'm figuring out the torso's texture (rock with cracks) and separating the pelvis into its own box part on the hip bone rather than relying solely on the chain sweep. Then I'm planning the chest armor plates as beveled boxes positioned over the pecs.

Still working out plate placement...

For the chest core, I'm thinking a small glowing hexagonal crystal embedded at front-center, surrounded by a ring of six tiny lava spikes radiating outward.

Then I add a ring of cone-shaped claws (ConeGeometry, tips pointing radially outward) at a slightly larger radius for a sunburst effect, plus a thin lava ring sweep between them, positioning everything just outside the surface so it reads as a pyro emblem on the torso.

I'm checking spacing so the core and spikes don't collide with the chest plates — the core sits at x=0 near y≈2.1 with spikes reaching radius ~0.21, while plates are placed at x≈±0.26-0.3, so I need to make sure the torso width at that height keeps them from overlapping.

Now I'm adjusting the plate width and offset slightly, narrowing them to around 0.24 wide centered at ±0.36 so they fit within the torso edge. I'm also thinking about adding glowing lava seams — using the painted cracks for vertical stripes, plus horizontal "abdomen rib" bands of lava between the hip and chest plates, built as a sweep along a loop on the spine.

I'm placing one lava belt near the belly and another lower near the hips, considering whether to break up the belly belt into basalt blocks with lava gaps in between rather than one continuous glowing ring.

I'm realizing the orientation issue — the sweep frame's tangent would make blocks extend along the loop direction instead of outward, which isn't what I want for the plates, so I need to rethink how the blocks are oriented relative to the body's surface normal.

Given the time budget, I'll simplify by sampling a point on the skin and grabbing its normal directly for placement, then focus effort on the major silhouette pieces rather than every small detail. For the shoulders, I'm planning tiered basalt pauldron plates (three stacked, decreasing boxes with rotation) topped with molten-tipped spikes at the shoulder joints, with thick gorilla-like arms running from shoulder to elbow to wrist using a heavy upper arm and forearm leading into oversized fists.

Writing arm chain polyline...

I'm reconsidering a sleeker golem design with gauntlet forearms, lava-crack paint details, and knuckle-spiked fists, then planning hand fingers as separate chains—five digits per hand with 2-3 joints each, angled downward and slightly spread for the rest pose.

Now I'm figuring out finger geometry and placement: tapered sweeps with rock-to-lava color bands for claw tips, a palm box positioned below the wrist, and finger offsets spread along the x-axis to attach naturally to the hand.

Checking proportions overall: wrist-to-fingertip reach, gorilla-like oversized arms, and total body height from feet through crest flame landing around 3.3 meters feels right for a floating golem silhouette. Now I'm setting up short thick legs with hip joints and defining the limb-building helper that handles root/target positions, segment lengths, and bend angles.

For the leg chain, I'm computing hip-to-ankle distance against the thigh and shin segment lengths, slightly bending the knee forward so the chain isn't perfectly straight. Writing leg geometry...

The tapered leg tube ends cleanly at the ankle so the foot sits flush with the floor. For the hips, I'm placing a pelvis box with front hanging tasset plates, a glowing lava belt, and lava vents along the back.

Now I'm adding a dorsal ridge of basalt spikes along the torso's back side, using angle 0 as the back-facing normal, with molten glowing tips and cracked seam textures across the spine.

I'm also considering a few small floating basalt shards orbiting near the shoulders as a stylized elemental detail, keeping them close to the body so they don't break height constraints.

Now I'm moving to shoulder armor, planning stacked pauldron plates attached to the chain's first joint on each side.

Between the plates I'm adding thin glowing lava boxes, plus three cones on top as spikes with lava tips. I'm placing the shoulder anchor near the torso's upper edge, with the pauldron center positioned slightly outboard, and attaching it explicitly to the arm's shoulder joint bone. I'm also considering a thick, sunken neck piece using a dark rock-colored hexagonal shape connecting the chest to the head, with hunched shoulders.

Now I'm defining the neck as a short two-point path leading forward and up to the head joint, tilting the head slightly forward while keeping the skull box world-aligned rather than tilted. I'm adding a large basalt hump on the upper back behind the shoulders with lava vents, plus the spike row, and now I'm writing a procedural rock paint function using cell noise to detect crack boundaries and color them with hot lava where the cell edges are thin.

I realize the units for the cell distance values are ambiguous -- I can't be sure if they're in meters or normalized cell units, which changes my crack-width thresholds dramatically, so I'm trying to reason through which interpretation gives plausible centimeter-scale crack widths before deciding how to normalize the calculation myself.

Instead I'm considering a cleaner approach: using a noise-contour method where I find where the noise value crosses near 0.5, producing natural winding crack lines without needing to guess the cell-distance units at all, possibly blending two noise octaves for more organic variation.

The smooth contours form closed loops that read as molten seams, which works well. For plates I want fewer cracks than the terrain, so I'll add a separate subtle plateRock paint with lighter crack intensity since plates use the same continuous world-space coordinates.

Paints themselves don't count toward the flat color budget, only materials do, so I can keep my palette tight: a few rock shades, lava, lava-hot, ember, and a dark tone. Since the material isn't emissive, lava needs to read purely through saturated color choice, and I'm considering a height-based gradient for the legs so the lower portions get a darker, ashier tint.

Writing color constants and paint functions...

Finishing the plate texture function...I need to double check that the paint callback's point parameter is typed correctly as a Vector3 so the noise function calls resolve properly, and confirm what type paint actually returns.

Now I'm sketching out the golem builder itself: setting up the hips joint as the spine root, then building the spine chain with catmull-rom points through the pelvis, lower spine, upper spine, and chest, assigning names to match the three spans. Next I'm starting the neck chain off the chest joint.

Now I'm sweeping the torso along the spine with a tapered box cross-section, shrinking toward the waist around t=0.35 and widening again toward the hips by t=0.85.

Adding pelvis and hip belt blocks...

Still writing spike placement logic...

Adding crystal spikes...

Defining arm radius taper...

I'm recalculating tier positions so adjacent tiers don't overlap, leaving a small visible gap where the thin lava slab can glow between them, then checking that the rotation applied to tilt the whole stack keeps that gap consistent on both tiers.

Now I'm adding three decorative spikes to the top pauldron tier, positioning their bases along the rim and giving each a slight angular offset and direction vector for a natural fanned-out look.

Then I'm placing a spike on the elbow joint itself, emerging from the back of the arm tube near the joint bone, angled outward and backward to give the armor a more aggressive silhouette.

For the forearm, I'm considering a gauntlet ring of small spikes placed around the arm's circumference at a fixed point along the chain, computing tangent frames so each spike sticks outward from the tube surface in a six-point knuckle-band pattern.

Then I'm working out a lava ring at the forearm, interpolating the arm's radius between its key points to get the correct band size and accounting for how polygon vertices sit slightly outside the face radius, so the sweep rides just above the surface without floating off.

Settling on a single spike ring near radius 0.245. Now I'm planning the hand geometry: a palm box positioned below the wrist joint, then four fingers plus a thumb, spacing finger bases evenly across the palm width.

Working out the finger joint positions, spreading each finger laterally with a downward curl toward a tip, and settling on three joints per finger (two spans plus a tip) rather than two, so each finger reads as knuckle-to-knuckle-to-claw tip.

Adjusting the finger geometry: shrinking radius and spacing so fingers don't overlap into a blocky fist, and sketching the thumb base positioned on the inner side of the palm depending on which arm is which.

I'm defining the thumb's offset positions relative to the wrist, parenting the finger joints to the arm's tip joint with a "digit" role, and considering adding knuckle crack paint and a small lava core glow on the palm for the hands.

Now shifting to legs: I'm computing hip and foot positions symmetrically for each side, using a limb helper to generate bent-knee joint chains with forward bending, checking the reach distance works for a 1.09 drop, then building the leg chain with hip/knee/ankle names and a "leg" role parented to the hips.

Still adding sweep radii and knee armor — placing a spike element offset from the knee joint to form a kneecap shape on top of the leg tube.

For the thigh plate, I'm thinking through how to position it using a surface ray-hit or nearest-point lookup against the leg sweep, since the thigh midpoint between hip and knee needs an accurate anchor rather than a rough guess.

Now I'm sketching the shin plate the same way, then moving to the feet — placing the foot box relative to the ankle bone with its heel extending behind and the sole resting at ground level.

Checking toe box placement against the foot top and confirming the bottoms sit flush at floor level. Now I'm moving on to the head, setting up a helper for positioning parts relative to the skull using forward/up/left offsets before building out the skull box itself.

Working out the jaw hinge position relative to the skull block, placing the lower jaw box so it spans slightly forward and below, and checking whether the overlap with the skull bottom leaves room for an open-mouth gap in the rest pose.

I'm now adjusting the jaw's rotation via a bone pose rotated 8° forward so the front drops and creates visible space, then inserting a small glowing lava box into that mouth gap and starting to place upper teeth as small cones.

Working out the brow rotation sign so the inner end (toward center) dips lower while the outer end lifts, giving that angry look on both sides. Then setting up hot-colored eye boxes positioned symmetrically with a matching tilt.

Checking the brow placement sits above the eye slits with proper overlap and a slight forward protrusion past the skull's face plane, while the eyes themselves recess just slightly under that overhang. Adding cheek spikes jutting from the jaw sides, skipping a chin plate for now, and starting to sketch the horn curves from the skull.

Defining horn bezier curves...

Tracing through the remaining edges to confirm the sawtooth polygon stays simple and non-self-intersecting before closing back to the start point.

I'm deciding to skip corner smoothing entirely to avoid crossing risks at the sharp flame tips, keeping it low-poly with a flat bevel. Now I'm setting up a smaller inner flame outline, scaled down for the hot core, positioned behind the horns.

The golem ends up around 3.5m tall with the flame on top, which feels appropriately imposing. For the floating shards, I'm attaching them rigidly to the hips bone and scattering eight of them in a ring using angle and radius variation for a loose, orbiting arrangement.

I realize the arms might collide with shards positioned near the sides, so I'm bumping the radius out slightly to clear the fists. For the shard geometry itself I'm considering a basalt octahedron with a lava-glowing underside, maybe pairing a dark top half with a hot-colored bottom cone to suggest molten rock.

I'm also thinking about whether the ground needs anything—skipping a full lava pool but adding a handful of small rubble rocks (dodecahedra) scattered near the feet, sunk slightly into the floor so they read as debris without breaking the "touches the ground" constraint.

Now I'm figuring out the chest core attachment: I'll grab the torso's surface after it's built, raycast from a point near the chest forward to find the front hit point, and throw if it comes back null so I catch bad placements early. Then I'm attaching a short hot-colored cylinder there with its axis aligned to the surface normal, embedding it slightly into the torso for a core-like protrusion.

I'm then adding rings of smaller lava-colored sticks and spike cones around that core hit point, sweeping them radially outward using the ring helper. I'm realizing the cone spikes need to sit with their axis along the radial direction in the surface plane, but with embed at 0.3 they'd end up half-buried into the torso since their center sits right at the surface level — so I'm considering lifting the item frames slightly outward to avoid that half-sunk look.

Now I'm adjusting the radii and sizes so the spike ring doesn't overlap the existing plates: shrinking the core cylinder, moving the lava ring inward, and pushing the plates outward to around 0.3–0.5 so everything fits without collision, while recalculating the torso's half-width taper at that height to make sure the plate placement still matches the body's silhouette.

Then I'm placing the chest plates using ray-casting against the torso surface at roughly (±0.4, 2.22), checking they land within the flat front face instead of clipping the rounded sides, and sketching out abdomen ridge rows at a couple of y-heights with small paired boxes to suggest ab plates beneath the chest core.

I'll skip loops since sweeps already cover the torso surface, and instead just add a lava belt slab at the waist, though it'd mostly be hidden within the torso's width.

Making the belt box slightly larger than the torso cross-section at that height so it protrudes as a thin glowing line. Then I'm planning a pelvis block for the hips sitting just below the belt, and ab rows above it, checking those don't collide with the core ring spikes.

Working out the ab plate dimensions and chest plate boxes, then considering a Genshin-style stylized palette with orange glow accents, and adding extra cracked lava detailing near the belly to break up the torso rock paint.

Checking that part colors accept Paint objects and that rotation/bone placement work correctly in model space, with flat geometry reserved for the octahedron pieces. I'm roughly tallying the total part count across torso, pelvis, abs, core, back, arms, and legs to gauge how heavy the merged model will be.

I'm verifying type signatures for part, spike, and limb helpers — making sure tuple arrays for color bands don't widen incorrectly, bone references match the Joint type, and offset/vector helpers behave as expected when generating leg points.

Now I'm sketching out the hand geometry, grabbing the wrist point and finding the arm's terminal joint, then sizing a palm box positioned relative to the wrist so it reads as a gauntlet slightly narrower than the forearm cap, planning a bigger knuckle block to balance the proportions.

Working out finger placement next, offsetting each of four fingers outward from center with splay and curl transforms, varying lengths per finger (longer middle, shorter pinky) to look natural, and considering small knuckle boxes before deciding the rounded sweep caps are enough on their own.

Now I'm naming joints consistently -- shoulder/elbow/wrist for arms, and indexed finger segments like index1/index2/index3 for digits, using index/middle/ring/pinky plus thumb as the finger set, and setting up leg tube sweeps with hexagonal cross-sections.

I'm working out the neck sweep geometry, making sure the cylindrical neck chain connects properly between the skull and torso without clipping through the jaw plate, using rock-colored material to tie it visually to the cracked skull surface.

Checking jaw position against the pauldron's top spikes — since head half-width is .26, there's no collision there. Now I'm checking the shoulder pauldron's horizontal extent, centered at x .7 with width reaching .37..1.03.

Verifying the arm starting point sits inside the pauldron's radius, confirming proper coverage. I'm setting up the jaw joint with its parent, pivot point, and aim direction, then checking that the rest pose keeps the jaw closed with a slight angle while teeth parts attach correctly to their respective bones.

For scattering rubble shards around the base, I'm deciding to skip any rng-based randomness since none is strictly required, and instead generate positions and sizes using deterministic angle and radius formulas for each shard index.

Still working out shard geometry... I'm using scaled octahedron geometries for jagged pieces, with rotation varied per shard index, plus adding a downward-pointing cone beneath each to suggest dripping lava.

Now I'm positioning the legs within the pelvis, adjusting hip x-offset to .33 so the thighs don't overlap, and tuning the toe rotation signs so each foot's toes fan outward correctly based on which side it's on.

Working through the ankle-to-leg bone chain naming, then setting up surface sweeps for the leg plates and a thigh plate box positioned using an interpolated point offset toward the front of the leg.

Checking the SDK's `limb` function return type — confirming it gives an array of Vector3 joint points so I can use `.clone()` and `.distanceTo()` on them directly. Moving on to defining the pelvis box dimensions.

Now I'm laying out the hip plate and tassets, naming the joint chains (spine, neck, head, jaw, arm, leg, digit) with shared paint for the plates. I need to work out the sweep function signature returning radius pairs, then place dorsal spikes along the torso using `b.along` with a spike generator function positioned between 12% and 70% of the sweep.

I'm positioning the back spikes to stop before the upper-back hump block, then adding a trio of hump spikes at staggered x positions with angled directions, plus two rows of lava vent boxes embedded into the hump's back face.

Now I'm structuring the final part-placement calls using the bone/position API, and working out how to feed the ring of hit points into the catmull curve helper so it sweeps a tube along the torso surface at the right radius.

Writing a `front` helper that raycasts into the skin and throws if no hit is found, then using it alongside `b.ring` and `b.sweep` to build the lava band encircling the forearm chain at a specific parameter along its length, sizing the ring radius to roughly match the arm's tube thickness there.

Then I'm placing a second ring of outward-facing cone spikes near the wrist, choosing a slightly smaller radius so the cones sit flush against the tapering tube geometry.

Checking ring orientation and stick flow defaults—both look fine, so I'm moving to finalize the full code: defining tier tuples, the paint function typed against Vector3 points, and a helper for head-local direction vectors.

Confirming sign conventions: left is positive X for brow tilt, eye rotation, cheek spike direction, and head offsets, all consistent. Horn bezier curves and skull geometry use these same head-local points, with jaw posing deferred to the end so other bone reads aren't affected.

Now I'm finalizing scattered rubble placement around the base using randomized positions and dodecahedron shapes, scaling their height by radius, while skipping extra lava seam details on thighs and pelvis plating since the knee spikes already cover that visual need. The function wraps up by returning the root bone.
